<location>https://stackoverflow.com/questions/76846664/github-action-self-hosted-runner-override-the-env-vars-how-can-i-configure-my</location>
<excerpt># Github action self-hosted runner override the env vars - how can I configure my own env vars? Tags: kubernetes, github, environment-variables, workflow, action - Score: 1 - Views: 1417 - Answers: 2 - Answered: yes - Asked by: EilonA (611 rep) - Asked: 2023-08-06 - Site: stackoverflow ## Question Github action self-hosted runner overrides the env vars It runs shell commands with --no-profile --norc so I can&`#39`;t add the env vars in the profile/bashrc files. I saw inside .env file that there are a few vars that are listed by env.sh under - varCheckList... How can I configure my own env vars without being overritten when an agent starts? ## Answers ### Answer by Joshua Pinter (score: 2) Update .env either manually or by running env.sh. You can update the .env file manually inside of the self-hosted runner&`#39`;s directory (adjacent to env.sh, run.sh and svc.sh. .env gets created when you first install the runner and picks up any of the key environment variables from your current session. This is done automatically by running env.sh. You can look at that script to see more details on what it&`#39`;s doing. This .env doesn&`#39`;t get overridden (as far as I&`#39`;m aware) after the runner has been installed so you are free to add variables in there manually. However, if you make changes to some key variables, like JAVA_HOME, and want .env to pick up those changes, it will not be done automatically. You need to first remove the existing .env file or if you have manual entries in there that you want to keep, you can just remove the outdated variables from that file and then run env.sh for it to generate a new .env file or update the existing one with any missing variables. NOTE: Running env.sh will not update any existing variables with the current values if the variable already exists in .env. Make sure your current session reflects the latest changes by starting a new terminal window or using source .zshrc (or similar). ### Answer by rvieira (score: -1) If you are using Linux, could be use the file /etc/environment to load your variables. In your host you can just put echo &`#39`;export MY_ENV=value&`#39`; >> /etc/environment</excerpt>
